newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan racketeer scandal claims new victim.
newsitem.headline: Japan racketeer scandal claims new victim.

text.p: A major scandal involving links between Japanese racketeers and financial institutions claimed a new victim on Sunday when a top bank enmeshed in the affair rescinded the appointment of a new president promoted to clean up the mess.
Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank (DKB) vice-president Ichiro Fujita joined a growing list of top Japanese executives who have seen their careers derailed over the past three months by the scandal.

Japanese government leaders, including Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, have used the high-profile investigation to also send a message to Japan Inc to clean up its corporate ethics ahead of next year's "Big Bang" deregulation of markets to make them again globally competitive.

The affair involves payoff loans to so-called "sokaiya" by DKB, Japan's third largest bank and Nomura Securities, its biggest brokerage, to stop the racketeers from disrupting their shareholders meetings by asking embarassing or sensitive questions about business affairs.
Fujita, whose admitted knowledge of the loans was defended by DKB when his promotion was announced, had been scheduled to take over on June 27.

On May 23, DKB announced its president, Katsuhiko Kondo, and chairman Tadashi Okuda were stepping down to take the blame for the bank's shady payoff loans to "sokaiya" Ryuichi Koike, the corporate racketeer at the heart of the scandal.
They were to be replaced by Fujita and vice-president Yoshiharu Mani as chairman.

Four other present and former DKB executives have been arrested on suspicion of giving 11.78 billion yen ($103 million) in collateral-short loans via a DKB affiliate to Kojin Building Co., a realtor run by Koike's younger brother, between July 1994 and September 1996 in violation of the Commercial Code.
Analysts said Fujita's fall from grace on the weekend was part of DKB's miscalculation of repercussions from the scandal.

Fujita, who under DKB's traditional management promotion system was automatically in line to take over the presidency, had made no secret of the fact that he was aware of loans to Koike's brother's company in late 1995 when he was the bank's managing director in charge of loan screening.
"The simplistic choice (of following traditional promotion procedures) has come back to haunt DKB," the Nihon Keizai Shimbun said on Sunday.
Kyodo News Agency quoted DKB sources as saying that Mani has also decided not to assume the chairmanship due to the widening of the scandal.
The affair has led to an increasing number of companies halting deals with DKB and an outflow of deposits from its branches across the nation.
Nomura's business has also suffered and the company faces the possibility that it may be ordered to suspend its business for up to six months for its links to racketeer Koike who is under arrest.

Prosecutors have indicted Nomura itself for violating the securities law by again illegally compensating Koike, as well as two former Nomura directors for violating both the securities law and the Commercial Code.
Former Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki has also been arrested and prosecutors have questioned former chairman Setsuya Tabuchi and former president Yoshihisa Tabuchi in connection with the scandal.
Speculation persists that the scandal may ensnare other financial firms and even politicians.
